description: Two-panel tensile-property figure for Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr (x = 0, 3, 6, 9 wt%) strips annealed at 550 °C for 5 h. (a) Engineering stress (MPa; ordinate 0–1000, ticks every 200) versus engineering strain (%; abscissa 0–50, ticks every 10), with a legend reading 0Cr (black solid), 3Cr (red dashed), 6Cr (blue dotted), 9Cr (teal dash-dot). All curves rise steeply from the origin; 0Cr then stays almost flat just below the 900 MPa line and ends with a vertical drop between the 20 and 30% gridlines; 3Cr starts lowest (between the 700 and 800 MPa gridlines) and creeps up to about the 900 MPa line, ending between the 30 and 40% gridlines; 6Cr keeps rising past the 900 MPa line and extends furthest, close to the 50% gridline; 9Cr climbs above the 1000 MPa gridline but terminates earliest, near the 20% gridline. (b) Dual-ordinate plot with the same four-entry legend: true stress (MPa; left axis 0–1500, ticks 300) and strain hardening rate (MPa; right axis 1000–4000, ticks 500) against an abscissa labelled "True strain (%)" with printed values 0.0–0.4. Each composition shows a smooth rising true-stress curve ending abruptly at fracture plus a separate noisy/decaying curve. Overall the figure shows Cr addition raises both strength and elongation of the annealed strips up to 6 wt% Cr, with 9Cr strongest but least ductile.

observations.observation: Panel (a) is an engineering stress-strain plot with engineering stress (MPa) on the ordinate (0–1000, ticks every 200) and engineering strain (%) on the abscissa (0–50, ticks every 10).
The legend of both panels identifies four conditions: 0Cr (black solid line), 3Cr (red dashed line), 6Cr (blue dotted line), 9Cr (teal dash-dot line).
In (a) the 9Cr (teal dash-dot) curve attains the highest stress, crossing above the 1000 MPa gridline, but terminates earliest, close to the 20% strain gridline.

In (a) the 6Cr (blue dotted) curve extends furthest along the strain axis, ending near the 50% gridline, whereas the 0Cr (black solid) curve ends with a near-vertical drop between the 20 and 30% strain gridlines.
In (a) the 3Cr (red dashed) curve starts at the lowest stress (between the 700 and 800 MPa gridlines) and rises gradually to about the 900 MPa gridline.

Panel (b) is a dual-ordinate plot: true stress (MPa) on the left axis (0–1500, ticks every 300) and strain hardening rate (MPa) on the right axis (1000–4000, ticks every 500), both against an abscissa labelled "True strain (%)" with printed values 0.0–0.4.

In (b) each Cr content is represented by two curves sharing a colour and line style (one smooth and monotonically rising, one noisy or steeply decaying), consistent with true stress read on the left ordinate and strain hardening rate on the right ordinate, although the figure does not label this mapping explicitly.
In (b) the black 0Cr solid true-stress curve terminates with a near-vertical drop just below a true strain of 0.2, the earliest termination in the panel.

The caption states the figure presents the tensile properties of Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr strips annealed at 550 °C for 5 h, with (a) engineering stress-strain curves and (b) true stress-strain and strain hardening rate curves.
The citing text states that annealing at 550 °C for 5 h significantly enhances the yield strength of all the strips, while Cr addition reduces the increment of yield strength.
The citing text states that after annealing the total elongation of the 0Cr strip obviously reduces while that of the 6Cr strip clearly increases.

The citing text states that with increasing Cr content the total elongation of as-cast strips gradually decreases, while that of annealed strips gradually increases except for the strip containing 9 wt% Cr.

The citing text states that the strain hardening rate is higher with increasing Cr content in the annealed strips and that, compared with as-cast strips, the strain hardening rate of all annealed strips except the 9Cr strip clearly decreases, with the 3Cr strip showing the largest reduction of about 500 MPa.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress-strain curves (stress 0–1000 MPa vs strain 0–50%) for annealed 0Cr (black solid), 3Cr (red dashed), 6Cr (blue dotted) and 9Cr (teal dash-dot). 9Cr reaches the highest stress (above the 1000 MPa gridline) but fails earliest (~20% strain); 6Cr reaches the largest strain (close to the 50% gridline); 0Cr is flat at ~900 MPa and drops vertically between 20 and 30% strain; 3Cr yields lowest (between 700 and 800 MPa) and rises to about 900 MPa.

Dual-ordinate true stress (left, 0–1500 MPa) and strain hardening rate (right, 1000–4000 MPa) plotted against true strain (printed 0.0–0.4), using the same 0Cr/3Cr/6Cr/9Cr colour legend. For each composition a smooth monotonically rising curve and a separate noisy or steeply decaying curve are present; the black 0Cr pair terminates with a near-vertical drop just below true strain 0.2. The mapping of individual curves to the left versus right ordinate is not explicitly labelled.

unreadable_items: panel (b): no printed annotation states which curves belong to the left (true stress) versus right (strain hardening rate) ordinate; the assignment is inferred from curve form only
panel (b): the abscissa is labelled "True strain (%)" but the printed tick values are 0.0–0.4, so the unit as printed is inconsistent (values are likely strain fractions)
panel (b): the individual noisy curve traces overlap at low true strain, so exact initial strain hardening rate values cannot be read
